items.title: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
items.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

items.title: Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText
items.summary: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText enables developers to efficiently train large language models across geographically distributed TPU slices by streaming parameter fragments instead of synchronizing full models at every step. This approach slashes cross-slice communication volume by over 60× and eliminates network stalls, allowing seamless multi-datacenter scaling without degrading model convergence or quality.

items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
items.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Accelerating development for massive Git repositories

items.title: Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies
items.summary: Semantic governance policies enable developers to govern AI agents by evaluating every proposed tool call inline before execution. Operating via Agent Gateway, the policy engine checks each action against user intent and plain-language rules to prevent unauthorized data sharing and prompt injection attacks. Developers can easily attach natural-language constraints to their agents and monitor auditable verdicts through Cloud Logging.

items.title: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver

items.title: From Files to Cited Answers in One API Call: Managed Ingestion and SearchDocuments in Agent Retrieval
items.summary: Agent Retrieval in Vertex AI introduces managed ingestion and SearchDocuments to replace custom chunking and embedding pipelines. Developers can now import document and video files directly from Cloud Storage and query them with a single API call for cited page numbers and timestamped results. The feature supports hybrid retrieval, metadata filtering, reranking, and multimodal video audio search.

items.title: Did the user ask for this? Securing AI agents against intent hijacking with Semantic governance policies
items.summary: Semantic governance policies protect AI agents from indirect prompt injection and intent hijacking by validating every proposed tool call against user intent and natural language constraints before execution. As demonstrated on the AgentDojo benchmark using a Gemini 2.5 Flash agent, this mechanism reduced attack success rates from 48.7% to 0.9% while maintaining high task utility. Developers can leverage these policies in preview within the Gemini platform via Agent Gateway to secure tool-use workflows.

items.title: Agent Anomaly Detection: Safeguarding agents across other clouds
items.summary: Agent Anomaly Detection now monitors ADK agents running across AWS, Azure, or on-premises by analyzing their traces and logs in your Google Cloud project. By ingesting OpenTelemetry-formatted data through the Telemetry API, it evaluates full conversations for behavioral drift without needing access to the agent's underlying runtime. This enables security teams to detect risks like rogue behaviors, tool misuse, and resource exhaustion across multi-cloud environments.

items.title: How to handle user, connector, and agent auth in Gemini Enterprise with a custom UI

These include authenticating users or workloads via Google Identity or Workforce/Workload Identity Federation, managing third-party 3-legged OAuth (3LO) for Federated Connectors through the Keystore, and configuring on-demand per-tool OAuth for custom ADK agents using Vertex AI Agent Engine and GCP Auth Manager.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: Building a Planar-Graph Floor Plan Room Solver in Pure TypeScript
items.summary: When a user drags walls on a 2D canvas—or uploads a hand-drawn sketch that gets parsed into approximate wall segments—you do not start with clean room polygons. You start with a messy soup of line segments: Endpoints that almost touch (2 to 6 inches apart) Walls drawn at 87.4 degrees instead of 90 degrees Interior partitions that terminate mid-span against an exterior wall (T-junctions) without sharing a vertex Two walls crossing in an X without a shared intersection node Half-walls and wing walls that dangle into an open living room without closing a face Nested freestanding closets or pantries sitting entirely inside a larger room If you try to run polygon detection straight on raw wall segments, room areas vanish, doors float off their host walls, and exterior square footage breaks. You do not need a multi-megabyte WebAssembly CAD kernel to solve this cleanly in the browser. A deterministic planar-graph pipeline in pure TypeScript handles the whole topology problem in under a millisecond on typical residential plans. items.title: Demystifying the 3-2-1 Backup Strategy: Protect Your Node.js App Data
items.summary: What is the 3-2-1 Backup Strategy? The 3-2-1 backup strategy is a foundational data preservation rule designed to protect applications from catastrophic data loss. It dictates that you must maintain 3 total copies of your data: 1 primary operational database and 2 additional backup copies. Furthermore, these copies must be stored across 2 different storage media types, with at least 1 copy located off-site in a separate physical or geographical location. By ensuring that no single system crash, hardware defect, or regional outage can destroy all your data simultaneously, this rule forms the backbone of modern disaster recovery planning. Imagine you possess irreplaceable personal records, such as your house deed and birth certificate. Keeping only the original document on your desk leaves you completely vulnerable to a coffee spill or accidental tearing. items.title: HybridCache in .NET 9
items.summary: Implementing a robust two-tier caching architecture in .NET traditionally meant hand-coding a complex dance between IMemoryCache and IDistributedCache (usually Redis). Engineers had to manually manage serialization overhead, implement double-checked locking to prevent cache stampedes, and write verbose invalidation logic across boundaries. This boilerplate frequently introduces race conditions under high concurrent load. .NET 9 introduces HybridCache, a unified abstraction designed to replace both IMemoryCache and IDistributedCache. items.title: Remotion vs. CoAnimator When Your Product Demo Needs an Update
items.summary: You publish a product demo on Friday. On Monday, the Save button moves into an overflow menu. You replace the recording. Now the caption appears before the click, the voiceover describes the old UI, and the next scene starts too soon. Someone has to fix all three before the video can go live again. That’s the edit I’d use to compare Remotion and CoAnimator. Both can work with coding agents. What matters after launch is whether the person who owns the video can make the change, review it, and verify the new export. In Remotion, the composition defines how the video looks and changes over time. Props can hold details that vary between exports, such as a release title, screenshot, or translated caption. If you expose those details as inputs, the next release can reuse the composition without a code change. items.title: How I keep context when switching between Claude Code, Codex and DeepSeek
items.summary: Every AI coding session I run ends in one of three ways: the usage limit hits, the session crashes, or I want to try the same task in another agent. All three lose the same thing: the agent's understanding of what's done, what's next, and what must not be touched. So the next session starts with me re-explaining the project. Or worse, with "continue where you left off" pointing at code that changed an hour ago. I built tagteam to make that handoff explicit, structured and checked against git. Here's the workflow, and the three design decisions that made it reliable. npm i -g tagteam-ai tagteam profile add claude # Claude Code with your normal login tagteam profile add deepseek # Claude Code on DeepSeek's API tagteam chain claude,deepseek tagteam # instead of `claude` Claude Code starts with the saved context. When it exits (for any reason), tagteam makes sure a handoff exists and asks: Continue with "deepseek"? [Enter]. Press Enter and the next agent starts with the task, the completed steps, the exact next action and your constraints. items.title: How We Verified 50,000 Email Probes for 10,000 Contacts Without Paying $400/mo
items.summary: If you build B2B prospecting or lead-enrichment software, you hit an uncomfortable math problem early: verifying 10,000 real business emails rarely means running 10,000 checks. When you test common personal patterns for a contact (first.last@, f.last@, first@, last@, contact@), you easily run ~5 checks per contact — 50,000 probes to land 10,000 verified emails. At typical instant email-verification API rates ($0.008–$0.01/check), 50,000 checks cost $400–$500 per run. Here is the exact architecture we built at Mailbase to run 50,000 probes cleanly at minimal cost without burning our sending IP. We run a strict cheap-to-expensive cascade: Syntax + placeholder filter (0 ms): discards typos, disposable domains, and theme leftovers (contact@yoursite.com). Cached DNS MX lookup (~15 ms, free): kills expired domains and RFC 7505 null MX (0 .). Persistent domain-facts cache (~2 ms, Postgres): Known catch-all domains are cached for 30 days (no point re-probing guessed patterns — a 250 OK proves nothing). Unreachable / refusing servers get a 6-hour cooldown so we never hammer a grumpy MX. Opening 5 separate TCP sockets to test 5 name permutations at acme.example looks like a dictionary attack

items.title: Give the agent the existing date formatter, not a one-off toLocaleString in the component
items.summary: The PR shows a timestamp with new Date(value).toLocaleString() or a handmade 'YYYY-MM-DD' slice. The repo already has a date formatter (formatDate, formatRelative, or an Intl wrapper) that the rest of the UI uses for locale, time zone, and relative phrases. The new string looks close in your browser and wrong in the next locale, or it disagrees with the same timestamp elsewhere on the page. I've started treating a one-off date format in a component as a consistency bug, not as a quick display. The existing formatter is there so list, detail, and emails do not invent three styles. JavaScript examples start with toLocaleString or a short slice. The model can write that without finding formatDate. Your helper may live under lib/date or next to i18n, which is easy to miss if the prompt only says "show the updated time." A second date library is a different problem. This one is narrower: the library (or Intl) is already wrapped, and the component bypasses the wrapper. items.title: Port 3000 is already in use on Windows: find it, end it, keep it from coming back
items.summary: "Port 3000 is already in use" (EADDRINUSE) means another process is listening on that port. On a dev machine it is usually a dev server that kept running after its terminal closed. Find the owner with netstat -ano | findstr :3000, check it with tasklist, and end it if it is a leftover. netstat -ano | findstr :3000 Look for a line in the LISTENING state. The last number is the process ID (PID). Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 3000 -State Listen | Select-Object LocalAddress, LocalPort, OwningProcess tasklist /FI "PID eq 12345" Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "ProcessId = 12345" | Select-Object Name, ParentProcessId, CommandLine The command line tells you which project and tool it is, for example node ... next dev or python -m uvicorn .... If it is a dev server you no longer need, end it and its child processes: taskkill /PID 12345 /T /F Or in PowerShell, for a single process: Stop-Process -Id 12345 Don't end a process you can't identify. If the owner is svchost.exe, System or a database you run on purpose, pick another port for your app instead. items.title: What a cold start actually costs on DigitalOcean Functions
items.summary: RevSofia, the car-meet planner I built for Sofia, runs its planning endpoint as a DigitalOcean Function. I'd never measured what the first call to a function costs compared with the ones after it, or whether ten requests arriving at once are any worse than one, so this week I did. I built a throwaway namespace with two trivial actions, one in Node.js 22 and one in Python 3.12, each just returning the current time, the process ID and how long that process had been alive. That last field turned out to be the most useful thing in the whole test, because DigitalOcean's activation record doesn't label cold starts explicitly. It gives you a waitTime annotation instead, and you have to work out what it means by watching the process uptime keep climbing. Coming from an Angular and .NET background with a strong OOP foundation, a lot of what I’m seeing feels surprisingly natural, though a few trade-offs definitely stand out. CLI & Boilerplate: The NestJS CLI feels very close to Angular’s—generating boilerplate quickly takes away a lot of the repetitive setup friction. Dependency Injection: Coming from .NET’s DI patterns, NestJS’s dependency injection feels familiar right away, including constructor-based injection. Decorators vs. Attributes: Decorators in Angular and NestJS (like @Injectable()) map closely to what you’d express with attributes ([MyAttribute]) in .NET. Modules Instead of Assemblies/Namespaces: Because TypeScript doesn’t have .NET’s namespaces, DLLs, or class libraries in the same way, NestJS groups and exports capabilities as modules—like UsersModule or CustomersModule. For replicated deployments, the docs describe shared MySQL storage and consistent key material; SQLite needs durable storage appropriate to the topology. The goal is not to collect more fields; it is to shorten the path from symptom to a testable explanation. Decide whether each replica shares telemetry, where persistent data lives, and how keys are rotated before scaling out. Start in a non-production environment, inspect a normal request and an edge case, and record what you would change before enabling the same configuration more broadly. Write down where the signal appears, who can see it, and what the next debugging step should be. If an engineer cannot make a decision from the captured event, revise the signal or its context. Validate the exact storage and networking design for your cluster; a mounted filesystem is not automatically safe for concurrent use. items.title: Continuations in Practice: What SE-0564 Split Continuations Changes
items.summary: Most iOS codebases still have callback APIs at their edges: an analytics SDK, a Bluetooth stack, a payment library, an old networking layer nobody wants to rewrite. Continuations are how those APIs become async functions. The conversion looks trivial, but it is the place I have seen the most subtle concurrency bugs: tasks that hang forever, crashes that only happen under load, and cancellation that silently does nothing. This article covers how continuations behave in real code, the three classic bugs (double resume, missing resume, ignored cancellation) and how to fix each one with today's APIs. It then covers what SE-0564: Split continuations changes. How the examples were checked: Today's APIs (CheckedContinuation, withTaskCancellationHandler, Mutex): every example was compiled and tested with Swift 6.2.4 in Swift 6 language mode (source on GitHub). The test suite includes 400 runs that deliberately race a timeout against completion and cancellation against completion. items.title: I built a local RAG server for Claude and Copilot in C#. Here is what I learned about search.
items.summary: I wanted Claude and GitHub Copilot to answer questions from my own notes and documentation, without uploading anything. So I built docs-rag-mcp, an MCP server in C# that indexes a folder of documents and lets any MCP client search it. You point it at a folder of Markdown, text, HTML, Word or PDF files. It splits them into passages, embeds each passage, and stores everything in one SQLite file. When you ask your assistant a question, it calls search_docs and answers from the passages it gets back, with the file and section for each one. claude mcp add docs-rag -- dnx DocsRagMcp --yes In VS Code and Cursor, the README has one-click install buttons. With Ollama, nothing leaves your machine. It also works with OpenAI and Azure OpenAI embeddings. Getting a basic pipeline working is the easy part. Making the results good is harder, and that is what this post is about. Most RAG tutorials cut text into fixed-size chunks. That loses the most useful piece of information a document has: which section a sentence belongs to. docs-rag-mcp splits Markdown, HTML and Word files at their headings first, and PDFs by page. items.title: Your HttpClient Retry Policy Probably Never Retried a Hung Request
items.summary: A phone is ringing, and your service has a couple of seconds to look the caller up in the CRM so the agent sees a name instead of a bare number. The CRM's first request hangs. You have a retry policy with three retries and exponential backoff, so you expect the second attempt to save you. It never runs. The call is answered with no context, and the logs show one TaskCanceledException. I found this pattern in my own public template, dotnet-integration-api-template. It sets http.Timeout = 10s on a typed HttpClient and adds a Polly retry with AddPolicyHandler. The retries work fine for fast failures (a 503, a refused connection). For a request that hangs, the whole 10 seconds goes to attempt one, and the retry loop is cancelled with it. So I built a small lab to measure exactly what each common wiring does. Every scenario uses the same fake upstream: attempt 1 hangs (30 s), and attempt 2 onwards answers 200 immediately. Every scenario has the same budget: 2 s for the whole call, 500 ms per attempt where a per-attempt timeout exists, 3 retries, 200 ms base backoff. items.summary: The most valuable thing I got from porting my first Android app to iOS wasn't the iOS app itself. It was everything I could reuse when I started the second one. I'm an independent app developer. I have two language-learning apps on Google Play, one for Hebrew and one for Korean. Both are built with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, with roughly 46,000 lines of Kotlin each. This autumn I ported both to native Swift and SwiftUI using Claude Code to write most of the code. The Hebrew app took 24 days from the first commit to the build I submitted to the App Store. The Korean app took five days of coding and 140 commits. It was live 14 days after the first commit. items.title: Why renaming survives source-generated COM
items.summary: Open a .NET assembly that exports a classic [ComVisible] COM object in a decompiler and the method names are right there — they have to be, because a COM client can late-bind through IDispatch and ask for "Add" by name at runtime. Obfuscation and COM have an old, uneasy relationship for exactly this reason: the wire contract is partly made of your identifiers. So it is worth knowing that the modern .NET COM path breaks that link entirely. An interface marked [GeneratedComInterface] can have every one of its names renamed to a single letter and the native contract does not move. What actually travels across a COM boundary — the method name, or the method's position? The answer decides whether renaming is safe, and it is different for the two COM paths .NET gives you. The classic path, [ComVisible(true)] plus a type library, carries names. A late-bound client calls IDispatch::GetIDsOfNames("Add") to turn the string into a dispatch id, then Invokes it. Rename Add to a and that lookup fails. The source-generated path introduced in .NET 8, [GeneratedComInterface], carries nothing but a GUID and an ordinal. items.title: OcctCSharpBridge 3.0: Bridging Open CASCADE 7.9.0 to .NET 8/9/10 for CAD & BIM Apps
items.summary: Integrating Open CASCADE Technology (OCCT)—the industry-standard open-source C++ B-Rep geometry kernel—into modern .NET (C#) desktop applications usually requires writing fragile, boilerplate-heavy C++/CLI glue code and manually managing OCCT's Handle(Standard_Transient) reference counting against the .NET GC. I open-sourced OcctCSharpBridge to provide a reusable OCCT 7.9.0 → .NET bridge for CAD, BIM, and engineering applications. items.summary: Longtime Slashdot reader AmiMoJo shares a report from The Guardian: For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned. This record hot streak, which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating. The daily global surface temperature rose to its highest ever point above preindustrial levels, 2.24C, on Monday, the most recent day for which data is available, and is forecast to persist at similarly high levels for at least several more days. "This will amplify the buildup of CO2 in the atmosphere driven by fossil fuel burning," said Richard Betts, the head of climate impacts research at the Met Office Hadley Centre. items.title: Tell HN: Lots of Ask HNs again
items.summary: There have been questions about why the /ask page (https://news.ycombinator.com/ask) was running dry of Ask HNs - e.g.: Ask HN: Why is Ask HN only showing me 14 posts? - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49984484 - Oct 2026 (47 comments) Ask HN: Why is pagination gone on "Ask HN", and showing only 19 items? - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50280719 - Oct 2026 (3 comments) I believe I found the problem. The pool of stories for https://news.ycombinator.com/ask has traditionally been drawn from the ranked stories list from which we generate the frontpage. That list is restricted to the top 1500 ranked submissions, and it seems the % of submissions which are text posts (i.e. no linked URL) had declined enough to starve the Ask HN feed. The solution is to compute a separate list of ranked Ask HNs. p.s. "Ask HN" is the conventional name but it means text posts. The title can also start with "Tell HN" or nothing in particular. [...] The company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. items.title: Turning an iPhone into a LiDAR, IMU and GPS Sensor
items.summary: Originally published at aharshit123456.space. In my first weeks at SMLab, NISER, in May 2024, before the ROS dashboard, I worked on a side track my notes call "iPhone Drone": use a LiDAR-equipped iPhone as the sensor head for a drone, for 3D mesh generation and SLAM. I wrote two iOS apps. DataSender (the SensorRecorder repo) reads the phone's motion sensors, GPS and LiDAR depth and streams them over TCP to a computer. LidarModel scans a space with ARKit and exports the reconstructed mesh as an OBJ file. items.title: Generating a claim-ready insurance PDF on-device in SwiftUI
items.summary: I make this app: Home Inventory, an iOS app for listing what you own room by room, with photos, prices, serial numbers and warranty dates. It is coming soon to the App Store. The feature everything else exists for is one button: produce a PDF you can send to an insurer after a fire, a flood or a burglary. There is no backend. The report is drawn on the phone, from data stored on the device (and in the user's own iCloud, only if they turn sync on). This post walks through how that PDF is built, with real code from the app. The renderer file is under 400 lines of Swift, and most of it is unglamorous layout arithmetic. The first decision was to make the PDF a pure function of plain values. The renderer does not know about SwiftData. But jurors acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy, a result that the company's lawyer said was a "profound rejection" of the government's narrative that it was corrupt from top to bottom and had a corporate culture of cheating, stealing and lying. Prosecutors had used the charge, commonly found in organized crime and drug cases, to accuse Huawei of operating illicitly to poach intellectual property and technological secrets from competitors and partners. The convictions covered allegations that the company did business in countries subject to U.S. sanctions — including Iran and North Korea — and made false statements to U.S. government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds. The patent is the latest signal of the AI video endgame: endless highly specific, customized content that is automatically generated based on the wealth of data companies and advertisers collect about you. Tech companies regularly file for patents that they don't end up actually putting into real products, but this one, called "creating a channel of video experiences tailored to a user," describes a system that many AI companies have been clearly trying to build. It imagines something called "My Channel," which would be filled with AI content generated based on demographic data, their video watch history (presumably from YouTube), and other information it knows about the user. items.title: Turn MacBook Trackpad Into a Speaker - Open Source Swift Tool
items.summary: TL;DR: This tool bypasses standard public haptic limitations by tapping into private macOS frameworks like MultitouchSupport. It takes generated speech, breaks it down into formants every 10 milliseconds, and translates those frequencies into precise sine tones played directly on the trackpad glass. Best for: Mac developers and tinkerers curious about macOS hardware internals and private APIs. Repository snapshot: ⭐ 1 760 stars · 🍴 89 forks · Swift · MIT Daily picks: Follow GitHub Open Source on Telegram nospeaker is a single-file Swift command-line utility that bypasses standard public haptic limitations on macOS. It taps into private frameworks like MultitouchSupport to drive a MacBook or external Magic Trackpad haptic motor at frequencies ranging from 98 Hz to 3,951 Hz, effectively turning the trackpad glass into a miniature speaker. The tool takes generated speech, breaks it down into formants and pitch every 10 milliseconds, and translates those frequencies into precise sine tones. Unvoiced sounds such as s, f, and t are converted into high-tone bursts, which are then played directly on the trackpad glass via rapid motor vibrations. Drives the trackpad motor up to 4,000 times

The FAA preliminary accident and incident notification briefly describes the incident as "UAS struck a fiber cable, a residential garage, and became entangled in power lines during takeoff." items.title: US Spy Agencies Suffer Breach of Some Unclassified Information
items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: The Central Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a cybersecurity breach that exposed some of their unclassified information, according to U.S. officials and other people familiar with the matter. The intrusions affected an open-source intelligence analysis system, a computer network that looks for intelligence insights in public, unclassified material, the people familiar with the issues said. It was not clear specifically what information was compromised, but classified material was not jeopardized, the people said. Information at other government agencies was also believed to have been exposed in the breach, according to two of the people. Open-source intelligence can include vast troves of commercially available data sets, social media content, satellite imagery and other online material. Much of it is publicly available, but it can include information sold by data vendors that can be highly revealing, especially when combined with other tranches of data. Spy agencies can also use the data alongside other sources of intelligence to inform analytical judgments.

items.title: What VP ≠ VNP Means (3 minute read)
items.summary: The Anthropic proof that VP≠VNP means that there is no way to find the permanent of a matrix of 0s and 1s if we are limited to arithmetic circuits of size polynomial in the input-size. This means that for P to equal NP, there must be some trick to computing permanents using AND/OR/NOT on the bits of the input that is better than addition and multiplication. There are many problems where access to Boolean operators is helpful, but it isn't clear how they would help with the permanent. There is a $1 million prize for a solution to this problem.

items.title: Recursive Self-Editing: LLMs Program Their Own Weight Edits for Self-Improvement (1 minute read)
items.summary: Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes, or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. SELFWRITE lets the model write its own weights. Each generation, the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives. It can raise gate accuracy and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees without a single gradient step.

items.title: Supercharging transformer residual connections (4 minute read)
items.summary: Google's DeepCrossAttention (DCA) enhances transformer residual connections by allowing each layer to dynamically select and route features from preceding layers, reducing information dilution and parameter count by 30-40%. Unlike traditional residual connections, DCA uses dynamic routing and depth-wise cross-attention mechanisms to achieve faster convergence and better quality with minimal parameter increase. Tested on large datasets like C4 and LM1B, DCA improves training efficiency and perplexity compared to standard models, proving a shift towards dynamic residual routing for scalable LLMs.

items.title: AI x Bio is not _just_ a data problem (14 minute read)
items.summary: How far AI gets in biology will depend largely on how much data we have. It will also depend on what is measured and the quality of that data. AI will likely become a powerful tool that will contribute to the study of biology, but there is still no clear path to documenting a comprehensive account of how a whole cell or tissue works.

items.title: The most important number in AI (42 minute read)

It is designed to be continuously updatable, and researchers can use it to look at trends going back years and forecast things for future models. items.summary: The BepiColombo mission is now preparing to swing into orbit around Mercury. items.title: On the Brutality of Amdahl's Law (12 minute read)
items.summary: The world is far too slow to see the high double-digit or more economic growth and seismic transformations in the economy that AI is predicted to bring. Intelligence isn't the only technology curve to go quasi-infinite in the last century and a half. Electricity, communication, computers, transportation, and agriculture have all experienced extreme growth and transformation. Despite this, we've only seen 2% GDP per capita growth for nearly 150 years.

items.title: AI, work from home, and the young-graduate job market (15 minute read)
items.summary: New college graduates are employed less than a few years ago. While AI may be a factor, there's growing evidence that work from home is an important factor moving the needle on young-graduate employment. AI exposure and teleworkability are highly correlated with each other, making it hard to distinguish definitively between the two factors. The full extent of AI's effects on the labor market might not manifest until the next recession.

items.title: Quark: our whole training stack, end to end, for $4,200 (7 minute read)
items.summary: Quark is a language model with about 165 million parameters trained for about $4,200 of compute (about 1,300 H-100-hours). It has the best benchmark average among open models of its size trained on similar token budgets. The model was created to explore every part of the training stack the team was using before spending serious money on a large model. This post looks at the model's data, architecture, pretraining at scale, context extension, reinforcement learning, evaluation, and release.

items.title: The avalanche that hit math is coming for AI development (50 minute read)
items.summary: AI's capabilities in mathematics exploded quickly. Current AIs can now complete well-scoped problems in mathematics easily. This ability to solve well-scoped problems is going to be an even bigger deal for machine learning research than for mathematics. AI labs mainly care about how any new algorithmic recipe empirically makes training more efficient or elicits smarter models - they don't care about theory for its own sake.
